33  Architecture

Plotje has a five-stage pipeline: pose -> draft -> plan -> membrane -> plot. Each stage is produced from the previous one by a single step. The user-facing functions pj/draft, pj/plan, and pj/plot are literal compositions of those steps, with pj/options folded in to inject pose-level options. Because the API is built as a composition, you can inspect each intermediate value and test each transition on its own.

This chapter introduces the single-step transitions, walks a small example through every stage, shows the user-facing functions as compositions, and explains how composite poses traverse the same pipeline through internal shape dispatch.

(ns plotje-book.architecture
  (:require
   ;; Clojure string -- splitting a message into sentences
   [clojure.string :as str]
   ;; Kindly -- notebook rendering protocol
   [scicloj.kindly.v4.kind :as kind]
   ;; Rdatasets -- standard datasets
   [scicloj.metamorph.ml.rdatasets :as rdatasets]
   ;; Plotje -- composable plotting
   [scicloj.plotje.api :as pj]
   ;; Plotje internals -- read in "The columns a layer reads" and "How Panels Share an Axis"
   [scicloj.plotje.impl.pose :as pose]
   [scicloj.plotje.impl.plan :as plan]
   ;; Membrane UI protocols
   [membrane.ui]))

Pipeline Overview

graph LR X["Raw data"] -->|pj/->pose| B["Pose"] B -->|pj/options pj/lay-* ...| B B -->|pj/pose->draft| D["Draft"] D -->|pj/draft->plan| P["Plan"] P -->|pj/plan->membrane| M["Membrane"] M -->|pj/membrane->plot| F["Plot"] style X fill:#eee,stroke-dasharray:3 3 style B fill:#d1c4e9 style D fill:#e8f5e9 style P fill:#fff3e0 style M fill:#e3f2fd style F fill:#fce4ec

Two terms used throughout: data space is values in their original units (centimeters, dollars, dates, species names); drawing space is the drawing-unit coordinates inside the output canvas. The plan stage holds geometry in data space; the membrane stage holds geometry in drawing space.

The five stages:

  • Pose – the composable specification you write. Built by pj/pose, pj/lay-*, pj/options, pj/facet, pj/arrange, pj/scale, and pj/coord. Lifted from raw data by pj/->pose, so a dataset can flow through the pipeline without an explicit constructor call. No computation has happened yet.

  • Draft – the pose flattened. A LeafDraft record holds :layers (a vector of one map per applicable layer with all scope merged in – :data, :x, :y, :mark, :stat, and aesthetic keys) and :opts (the pose-level options that flow into the plan stage). A composite pose produces a CompositeDraft instead, carrying per-leaf drafts (:sub-drafts), the resolved composite-framing geometry (:chrome-spec), the layout map from leaf path to rect (:layout), and the composite’s overall dimensions (:width, :height). Produced by pj/pose->draft.

  • Plan – fully resolved geometry in data space (domains, ticks, legends, computed shapes). A Plan record (composite plots use CompositePlan) holding panels as plain maps, layers as PlanLayer records, and numeric arrays as dtype-next buffers. Produced by pj/draft->plan. No rendering primitives yet.

  • Membrane – a PlotjeMembrane record carrying positioned drawing primitives (Translate, WithColor, Path, Label, …) in drawing space, sized to the output canvas. The record itself implements the Membrane library’s UI protocols, so it composes with other Membrane elements. Produced by pj/plan->membrane. The Membranes chapter walks this stage in depth.

  • Plot – rendered output (SVG hiccup or BufferedImage). Produced by pj/membrane->plot, dispatching on a :format keyword.

The composition shortcuts pj/draft, pj/plan, pj/membrane, and pj/plot run the chain from a pose up through the named stage. They are introduced one section down.

Most users only interact with the pose stage and never need to think about the others. The stages below matter when you are debugging unexpected output, building a custom renderer, or extending the library.

Why these stages?

A simpler library could go from data to a rendered image in one function. Plotje splits the work into five stages so each stage addresses a distinct concern, and each boundary between stages has a specific purpose:

  • The pose is what the user specifies.

  • The draft is the same specification flattened, with scope merged in. This boundary lets the layer engine run on a uniform input regardless of how the pose was built (single layer, faceted leaf, composite tree).

  • The plan holds geometry in data space – domains, ticks, computed shapes – before any drawing. This boundary lets you inspect and validate plot structure with Malli, and it lets multiple renderers share the same computed plan. It also carries the dimensions the layout settled on, so where each panel will sit on the canvas is decided here: pj/frames reports it, and the membrane stage draws into it.

  • The membrane holds drawing primitives in drawing space. This boundary decouples “what to draw, where” from the output format, so SVG and raster renderers consume the same membrane tree.

  • The plot is the format-specific output: SVG hiccup, a BufferedImage, or any other format a backend supports.

This structure has two consequences. Every intermediate value can be inspected with kind/pprint. The same pipeline can be extended by registering new methods at any stage – mark, stat, scale, coordinate system, output format – without modifying the core. The Extensibility chapter walks each extension point.

The Single-Step Transitions

Each transition is its own public function. Walk the example below to see what enters and what leaves at each step. The per-function reference (arities, arguments, return types) lives in the API Reference.

Step 1: pj/->pose

Lift raw data (or a pose) to a pose. Polymorphic on input: a dataset becomes a leaf pose with :data set; an existing pose flows through unchanged (idempotent). This is the structural lift that lets every downstream function accept either raw data or a pose. It stops there – it sets no mapping. The default mapping that makes a bare dataset render is filled in when the pose is drafted, and pj/infer-mapping writes it onto the pose ahead of that (see “Where Inference Happens” below).

The example traced through every stage is iris petal measurements, with a scatter and per-species regression line. Pose-level :x, :y, and :color mappings; two layers on top of that mapping.

(def trace-pose
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/pose :petal-length :petal-width {:color :species})
      pj/lay-point
      (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model})))

The pose auto-renders as the plot it specifies:

trace-pose

The underlying value is a plain Clojure map – kind/pprint reveals the structure (without it, the auto-render would re-show the plot):

(kind/pprint trace-pose)
{:mapping {:color :species, :x :petal-length, :y :petal-width},
 :layers
 [{:layer-type :point} {:layer-type :smooth, :stat :linear-model}],
 :data

Step 2: pj/pose->draft

Flatten a pose into a draft. For a leaf, returns a LeafDraft record carrying the merged layer maps and the pose-level options. The pose-level mapping (:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width, :color :species) appears inside each of the two layer maps, alongside layer-specific keys (:mark, :stat). The layer engine downstream receives a uniform shape regardless of where each mapping was originally specified. Keys prefixed with double underscores (e.g. :__panel-idx) are internal markers; they pass through the plan stage and follow the Clojure “do not consume” convention.

A draft layer’s :data carries one column the pose was not given: :scicloj.plotje/row, the row of the pose’s dataset each row came from. A facet splits the data and a series pivots it, and either numbers the resulting rows from zero again, so the row number is attached before both. :brush true reads it, which is how highlighting a point in one panel highlights the same row in the others. Like the double-underscore keys, the column is Plotje’s: no mapping can name it, and no list of available columns shows it.

(def trace-draft
  (pj/pose->draft trace-pose))
(kind/pprint trace-draft)

Step 3: pj/draft->plan

Resolve the draft into computed geometry. Reads :opts from the draft to apply title, dimensions, axis labels, and so on. The smooth layer’s :linear-model stat resolves into per-species line segments here; the point layer keeps the raw observations grouped by species. The legend gets one entry per species.

(def trace-plan
  (pj/draft->plan trace-draft))

The plan – a Plan record carrying panels, total dimensions, ticks, the legend spec, and per-layer geometry (groups of dtype-next buffers):

(pj/valid-plan? trace-plan)
true

Step 4: pj/plan->membrane

Convert the plan into a PlotjeMembrane – a tree of membrane drawing primitives positioned in drawing-space coordinates, wrapped in a record that itself implements the Membrane UI protocols (IOrigin, IBounds, IChildren).

(def trace-membrane (pj/plan->membrane trace-plan))

The membrane carries the rendered drawables plus the canvas size and title. The drawables sit inside the record’s :drawables field; record fields :width and :height give the canvas size; and :plotje/title carries the title (when set):

(kind/pprint trace-membrane)

   :y 181.0,

     :drawables

       :font
       {:name nil, :size 13, :weight nil, :width nil, :slant nil},
       :text-anchor "middle"})}}}

   :y 382.0,

The dedicated Membranes chapter walks the record’s protocols, the namespaced-attribute convention, and how a PlotjeMembrane composes with hand-built Membrane elements.

Step 5: pj/membrane->plot

Convert the membrane into the rendered output for a chosen format. Dispatches on the format keyword; :svg is built in. This is the only stage whose output is format-native rather than portable: every earlier stage is the same across backends, while here the membrane becomes SVG hiccup, a BufferedImage, or another format’s bytes. The membrane carries its plan-derived dimensions as record fields (read via (membrane.ui/width m)/(height m)), so pj/membrane->plot does not need them respelled in opts:

(def trace-plot
  (pj/membrane->plot trace-membrane :svg {}))
(kind/pprint trace-plot)

Pipeline Shortcuts: pj/pose, pj/draft, pj/plan, pj/membrane, pj/plot, pj/save

Each pipeline stage has a user-facing convenience that runs the chain from raw input up through that stage; pj/save is the file-output sibling that runs the chain all the way and writes the result to disk:

  • pj/pose – not a literal composition. On raw data its one-argument form is pj/->pose. With more arguments it reads column arguments ((pj/pose data :x :y)) and a mapping, and on an existing pose it merges them into that pose’s mapping. It infers nothing: the default mapping is filled in when the pose is drafted.

  • pj/draft – raw input -> draft.

  • pj/plan – raw input -> plan.

  • pj/membrane – raw input -> membrane tree.

  • pj/plot – raw input -> rendered figure.

  • pj/save – raw input -> file on disk (renders, then writes).

Each shortcut starts from raw input and stops at a different stage along the same chain. The solid line is the stage-to-stage pipeline; each dashed arrow is one shortcut, running from raw input up to the stage it produces:

graph LR X["Raw data"] --> B["Pose"] --> D["Draft"] --> P["Plan"] --> M["Membrane"] --> F["Plot"] X -.->|pj/pose| B X -.->|pj/draft| D X -.->|pj/plan| P X -.->|pj/membrane| M X -.->|pj/plot| F style X fill:#eee,stroke-dasharray:3 3 style B fill:#d1c4e9 style D fill:#e8f5e9 style P fill:#fff3e0 style M fill:#e3f2fd style F fill:#fce4ec

The shortcuts from pj/draft on are near-literal compositions of these steps: each lifts raw input with pj/->pose, applies the shared pj/infer-mapping step (which gives a pose that names no :x or :y column the default mapping of its data, and changes nothing on a pose whose mapping names one), and runs the chain up to its stage. Their source shows the pipeline directly. Two things are simplified below for clarity: the pj/->pose caller-name argument – which only tunes error messages – is elided, and pj/pose is shown at its 1-arity (its other arities also read column arguments and a mapping).

Pseudocode:

(defn pose         ; 1-arity; the other arities also read
  ([x]             ; column arguments and a mapping
   (-> x
       ->pose)))

(defn draft
  ([x]
   (-> x
       ->pose
       infer-mapping
       pose->draft))
  ([x opts]
   (-> x
       ->pose
       (options opts)
       draft)))

(defn plan
  ([x]
   (-> x
       ->pose
       infer-mapping
       pose->draft
       draft->plan))
  ([x opts]
   (-> x
       ->pose
       (options opts)
       plan)))

(defn membrane
  ([x]
   (let [pose (-> x
                  ->pose
                  infer-mapping)
         opts (:opts pose {})]
     (-> pose
         pose->draft
         draft->plan
         (plan->membrane opts))))
  ([x opts]
   (-> x
       ->pose
       (options opts)
       membrane)))

(defn plot
  ([x]
   (let [pose (-> x
                  ->pose
                  infer-mapping)
         opts (:opts pose {})
         fmt  (or (:format opts) :svg)]
     (-> pose
         pose->draft
         draft->plan
         (plan->membrane opts)
         (membrane->plot fmt opts))))
  ([x opts]
   (-> x
       ->pose
       (options opts)
       plot)))

(defn save
  ([x path] (save x path nil))
  ([x path opts]
   (let [pose (-> x
                  ->pose
                  infer-mapping)
         pose (if opts (options pose opts) pose)
         fmt  (resolve-format pose path)]  ; :format opt, else path extension
     ;; render the plan to fmt bytes and write them to path
     (write-file path (plan->plot (plan pose) fmt (:opts pose)))
     path)))

In plot, the let binds pose, opts, and fmt for use in the subsequent -> thread, which runs the four transitions (pose->draft, draft->plan, plan->membrane, membrane->plot) in order. The membrane carries the dimensions the plan settled on as record fields, and the title under :plotje/title, so membrane->plot reads them without the plan.

pj/save is the file-output sibling: it lifts and infers the same way, resolves the file format (from a :format option or the path extension), renders the plan to those bytes, and writes them to disk, returning the path. resolve-format and write-file above stand in for that format-resolution and file-writing detail.

The 2-arity of each function folds the options map into the pose using pj/options before recursing into the 1-arity.

pj/membrane is the analogous shortcut for the membrane stage, useful for consumers that want a membrane tree without choosing an output format yet – for example a custom backend, or a target that Membrane supports but Plotje has not wired in yet.

Because the compositions call the steps, redefining a step (with with-redefs for testing, or with a custom defmethod for plan->membrane) takes effect in every user-facing function.

The composition holds at runtime:

(let [pose-with-opts (-> trace-pose
                         (pj/options {:title "Iris Petals"
                                      :x-label "Petal length"
                                      :width 700}))
      via-plan (pj/plan pose-with-opts)
      via-arrows (-> pose-with-opts
                     pj/->pose
                     pj/pose->draft
                     pj/draft->plan)]
  {:title-match (= (:title via-plan) (:title via-arrows))
   :x-label-match (= (:x-label via-plan) (:x-label via-arrows))
   :width-match (= (:width via-plan) (:width via-arrows))
   :title (:title via-plan)
   :x-label (:x-label via-plan)
   :width (:width via-plan)})
{:title-match true,
 :x-label-match true,
 :width-match true,
 :title "Iris Petals",
 :x-label "Petal length",
 :width 700}

Plot-level options (title, x-label, width, …) are stored on the pose’s :opts, copied into the LeafDraft’s :opts, and read by pj/draft->plan. Calling the steps directly, without the user-facing convenience, produces the identical plan.

The same property allows inspection at any stage: stop the chain before the next step. (-> data ... pj/pose->draft kind/pprint) shows the draft; (-> data ... pj/pose->draft pj/draft->plan) shows the plan.

Where Inference Happens

Two of the steps also infer: they fill in choices the user did not specify. Inference is what lets a dataset alone – with no mapping, no layers, no options – produce a complete plot. Most one-line examples in this book rely on inference at one or both of these stages. The Inference Rules chapter is the authoritative reference for what each stage infers.

(pj/pose {:x [1 2 3 4 5]
          :y [2 4 3 5 4]
          :g [:a :a :b :b :b]})

Where each kind of inference lives:

  • Mapping inference fills in :x, :y and :color from the first one to three columns of the data: one column to :x, two columns to :x and :y, and a third column to :color. It runs in pj/pose->draft, after a facet over columns is expanded into cells, on every leaf, cells of a composite included. It writes the default where neither the pose’s mapping nor any layer names an :x or a :y column, and where the first layer names no column, whatever the later layers name (the example below this list shows a later layer naming the default’s columns). pj/infer-mapping is the same step as a public function: it writes the default onto the pose, where it can be read before drafting. pj/->pose, pj/pose and the pj/lay-* functions read no column of the data when they are called: a layer naming no column is given its columns when the pose is drafted, and a layer left without a column is reported then.

  • Layer-type inference is written into the draft. A pose with no pj/lay-* call is given one layer, of the type its columns choose: a categorical x with a numerical y gives a boxplot, a temporal x with a numerical y gives a line, a numerical x and y give a scatter, and one numerical column gives a histogram. pose/elaborate makes the choice, so the draft layer already holds its :mark and :stat. pj/draft->plan chooses the stat of a layer whose type leaves it open – a bar with no :y column counts – and gives a draft layer written by hand with no :mark the type its columns choose.

  • Column-type inference lives in pj/draft->plan. :x-type/:y-type/:color-type default from the data (numerical / categorical / temporal); a user-supplied :x-type overrides the default.

  • Geometry inference lives in pj/draft->plan. Domains default to data ranges; ticks default to evenly-spaced values; legend entries are derived from the layers’ aesthetic mappings; the coordinate system defaults to :cartesian.

Mapping inference and the choice of a layer type run in pj/pose->draft; the rest runs in pj/draft->plan. Every inferred default has an explicit override (pj/scale, pj/coord, pj/options, mapping keys like :x-type), so the user can opt out of any single inference without losing the others.

Below, pj/pose->draft gives a pose built by pj/->pose the default mapping of its three columns, with no pj/infer-mapping call in between. The points keep the color of the default beside a smooth that names the default’s :x and :y columns:

(->> (-> {:a [1 2 3 4] :b [2 4 3 5] :c ["u" "u" "v" "v"]}
         pj/->pose
         pj/lay-point
         (pj/lay-smooth :a :b)
         pj/pose->draft)
     :layers
     (mapv #(select-keys % [:mark :x :y :color])))
[{:mark :point, :x :a, :y :b, :color :c}
 {:mark :line, :x :a, :y :b, :color :c}]

The columns a layer reads

One choice is made in pj/pose->draft, after a facet over columns is expanded into cells, by pose/elaborate: which columns a layer reads where it names no column, or names a column on only one of the two axes. A pj/lay-* call keeps its columns on its own layer, so the pose below has no mapping. Its panel’s columns are, on each axis, the column of the first layer that names a column on that axis. pose/elaborate writes them into each layer that needs them, and the draft then merges the pose’s mapping and each layer’s mapping by scope and nothing else:

(-> {:week [1 2 3 4]
     :adults [30 25 28 35]
     :children [20 15 18 22]}
    (pj/lay-point :week :adults)
    (pj/lay-line {:y :children})
    pj/lay-smooth
    pose/elaborate
    (dissoc :data)
    kind/pprint)
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-line names :children on :y where this pose draws :adults on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per column, write (pj/facet pose {:y [:adults :children]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

{:layers
 [{:layer-type :point, :mapping {:x :week, :y :adults}}
  {:layer-type :line, :mapping {:x :week, :y :children}}
  {:layer-type :smooth, :mapping {:x :week, :y :adults}}]}

The column is written into the layer and not into the pose’s mapping. Written into the pose, it would reach every layer by scope, and a layer type that can draw from one column – a bar that counts, a histogram – would be given a second column it did not ask for. The panel’s columns are written into the pose in one place, a facet over columns: its cells are made from the panel’s columns, with the facet’s column on the axis it names (pose/expand-facet-nodes, below). Elaboration also writes into the pose’s mapping the default mapping of data with one to three columns and the columns of a pivoted series, and it turns a column named on :y alone on its side (see “A column on :y alone” below).

The panel’s columns are also what a pj/lay-* call on a composite compares its columns with, to find the cell the layer joins: pose/last-matching-leaf-path reads pose/leaf-place, the function pose/elaborate reads. A cell built by pj/lay-* names its columns on its layers and not in its mapping. Such a cell is matched by its columns all the same, because the panel’s columns are read from the layers where the mapping names none.

A layer may reach the plan with no data at all: a template drawn before pj/with-data, or a cell added to an arrangement whose root has no data. plan/resolve-panel-draft-layers gives such a layer a dataset of no rows before its stat runs, so every stat takes the route it takes for data that is all missing, and the panel reads “no data”.

What elaboration writes

pose/elaborate writes into a pose what the draft would otherwise have to choose, in this order: the rows the pose keeps (apply-where); a series pivoted into a key column and a value column; the default mapping of data with one to three columns; one layer, where the pose names columns and has no layer; the panel’s columns, into each layer that reads them; a layer type for each layer left to inference; and the flip of a column named on :y alone, described in the next section.

A layer naming no column is given both of the panel’s columns. A layer naming one column is given the other only where its layer type cannot draw from one column, which layer-type/column-counts says. The line naming :children above is given :week. A bar naming :day beside points of :day against :visits is given nothing, and counts:

(def counted-beside-points
  (-> {:day ["mon" "tue" "mon" "wed"]
       :visits [3 5 2 4]}
      (pj/lay-point :day :visits)
      (pj/lay-bar :day)))
(->> counted-beside-points
     pose/elaborate
     :layers
     (mapv :mapping))
[{:x :day, :y :visits} {:x :day}]

A second call to pose/elaborate changes nothing, so the draft can run it on a pose that was elaborated already.

A column on :y alone

A histogram, a density, a rug and a counting bar draw from one column, which their stat reads on :x. Where a pose names a column on :y and none on :x, in its mapping or in its layers, and every layer can draw from one column, pose/elaborate moves the column to :x and writes :coord :flip into the pose’s options, so the marks run along the vertical axis:

(-> {:height [1.6 1.7 1.8 1.7 1.75]}
    (pj/lay-histogram {:y :height})
    pose/elaborate
    (dissoc :data)
    kind/pprint)
{:layers [{:layer-type :histogram, :mapping {:x :height}}],
 :opts {:coord :flip}}

A layer that draws only from two columns, or that names an :x, keeps the pose as it is written, and the layer left with no :x column is then reported. A :coord other than :flip on a pose that would be turned on its side reports an error, since such a pose can be drawn only with the coordinates flipped. A layer type of an extension takes part by declaring :column-counts.

The color a layer is given

Where the layers of a pose draw different columns, nothing on the panel says which marks belong to which columns. pose/leaf->draft gives each layer a label made of the columns the layer draws (pose/overlay-labels), and each axis is titled with the columns of every layer. Each layer whose mapping specifies no :color is then given its label as a color: one palette color and one legend entry per layer. A layer that specifies a color keeps that color. On a panel where a layer is colored by a column, no layer is given the default, because the legend of that panel lists the column’s values. The color is written into the draft and not into the pose: each draft layer below maps :color to a column of labels the draft adds to its data, except the smooth, which keeps its black:

(def sepals-and-petals
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width)
      (pj/lay-smooth {:color "black"})))
(->> sepals-and-petals
     pj/draft
     :layers
     (mapv (fn [layer]
             (let [color (:color layer)]
               (if (keyword? color)
                 (first ((:data layer) color))
                 color)))))
["sepal length / sepal width" "petal length / petal width" "black"]

Composite Poses

A composite pose – one with :poses inside – flows through the same steps. Each step dispatches internally on shape: a leaf pose produces a LeafDraft; a composite pose produces a CompositeDraft. The user-facing pipeline is unchanged.

(def composite-pose
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/arrange [{:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}
                   {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}])
      (pj/pose {:color :species})))
composite-pose

pj/draft (the composition of ->pose, infer-mapping and pose->draft) returns a CompositeDraft – wrap in kind/pprint to inspect:

(-> composite-pose pj/draft kind/pprint)
{:width 600,
 :height 400,
 :sub-drafts
 [{:path [0 0],
   :rect [0.0 0.0 240.0 400.0],
   :draft
   [{:y :petal-width,
     :stat :identity,
     :color :species,
     :__panel-idx 0,
     :mark :point,
     :color-scale
     {:values
      {"setosa" "#E41A1CFF",
       "versicolor" "#377EB8FF",
       "virginica" "#4DAF4AFF"},
      :type :linear},
     :layer-type :point,
     :__scale
     {:color
      {:values
       {"setosa" "#E41A1CFF",
        "versicolor" "#377EB8FF",
        "virginica" "#4DAF4AFF"}}},
     :x :petal-length,
     :__color-order ["setosa" "versicolor" "virginica"],

The composition holds for both leaf and composite poses – pj/plan is (-> pose pj/->pose pj/pose->draft pj/draft->plan) either way – because each step dispatches on shape at the bottom of its call.

The composite path also performs work across leaves that a single leaf has no counterpart for: deciding which cells share an axis, and what that axis covers. The next section follows it through the stages.

How Panels Share an Axis

Panels that are meant to be compared are drawn on one axis: the same numbers, or the same categories, in every panel. Plotje draws several panels in two ways, and both follow one rule: a shared axis covers what the panels sharing it draw.

  • A facet by the categories of a column is one plan with several panels.

  • An arrangement, and a facet over columns, is a CompositePlan: one plan per cell.

The same two clinics drawn by each path:

(def north
  {:week ["w1" "w1" "w2" "w2"]
   :age ["adults" "children" "adults" "children"]
   :visits [30 20 25 15]})
(def south
  {:week ["w1" "w1" "w2" "w2"]
   :age ["adults" "children" "adults" "children"]
   :visits [60 45 50 40]})
(def arranged-clinics
  (pj/arrange [(pj/lay-bar north :week :visits {:color :age :position :stack})
               (pj/lay-bar south :week :visits {:color :age :position :stack})]
              {:share-scales #{:y}}))
arranged-clinics
(def faceted-clinics
  (-> {:clinic ["north" "north" "north" "north" "south" "south" "south" "south"]
       :week ["w1" "w1" "w2" "w2" "w1" "w1" "w2" "w2"]
       :age ["adults" "children" "adults" "children"
             "adults" "children" "adults" "children"]
       :visits [30 20 25 15 60 45 50 40]}
      (pj/lay-bar :week :visits {:color :age :position :stack})
      (pj/facet :clinic)))
faceted-clinics

The pose stage decides which cells share

pj/pose->draft reads the composite’s :share-scales and puts the cells into groups. It measures no extent to do this. It reads the type of each column, to report cells that cannot share, and for a column of categories the order the data holds them in, which the group carries as :order. Each sub-draft carries the groups of its cell under :share, by axis:

(->> arranged-clinics
     pj/draft
     :sub-drafts
     (mapv :share))
[{:y {:group 0}} {:y {:group 0}}]

Two cells are placed in one group where they draw the same thing along an axis: the values of one column, or what a stat computes from one column – a count, a density – which the stat declares (see What a stat computes). A count of a column and the values of that column are never in one group. :share-scales is a set of axes, as above, or a map from an axis to :same-column, to the columns that go together on that axis, {:y [[:hwy :cty]]}, or to :all, {:y :all}, which puts together every cell that draws the same kind of thing on that axis – values with values, counts with counts, densities with densities.

:share-scales names an axis as it is drawn: :x is the horizontal axis. The groups are recorded by the axis of each cell’s own mapping, so two flipped cells sharing :x are in a group on their :y, which is the column that runs across:

(->> (pj/arrange [(pj/coord (pj/lay-bar north :week :visits) :flip)
                  (pj/coord (pj/lay-bar south :week :visits) :flip)]
                 {:share-scales #{:x}})
     pj/draft
     :sub-drafts
     (mapv :share))
[{:y {:group 0}} {:y {:group 0}}]

With no :share-scales written, cells that split the data of one pose – the cells of (pj/arrange data [...]) and of a facet over columns – share each axis on which two of them draw one column. Below, the two cells draw :week on :x and share it, and the group lists the weeks in the order of the data’s rows:

(->> (pj/arrange {:week ["w2" "w1" "w2" "w1"]
                  :adults [30 25 28 35]
                  :children [20 15 18 22]}
                 [{:x :week :y :adults} {:x :week :y :children}])
     pj/draft
     :sub-drafts
     (mapv :share))
[{:x {:group 0, :order ["w2" "w1"]}}
 {:x {:group 0, :order ["w2" "w1"]}}]

Poses that carry data of their own, arranged with (pj/arrange [pose-a pose-b]), share no axis unless :share-scales names it, as the two clinics above do. A cell whose layers draw two columns on an axis belongs to the groups of both columns, and the two groups become one: three cells sharing :y, drawing :adults, :children, and both, are one group.

(def weekly-visits
  {:week [1 2 3 4]
   :adults [30 25 28 35]
   :children [20 15 18 22]})
(->> (pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point weekly-visits :week :adults)
                  (pj/lay-point weekly-visits :week :children)
                  (-> weekly-visits
                      (pj/lay-point :week :adults)
                      (pj/lay-line :week :children))]
                 {:share-scales #{:y}})
     pj/draft
     :sub-drafts
     (mapv :share))
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-line names :children on :y where this pose draws :adults on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per column, write (pj/facet pose {:y [:adults :children]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

[{:y {:group 0}} {:y {:group 0}} {:y {:group 0}}]

The plan stage decides what the axis covers

What a cell draws is known only after its stats have run. A stack of bars reaches the sum of its parts, which no row of the :visits column holds. So pj/draft->plan first measures every sharing cell: plan/draft->extents runs the cell’s stats and returns the extent the cell draws on each axis, before any padding.

(->> arranged-clinics
     pj/draft
     :sub-drafts
     (mapv (fn [sub-draft]
             (plan/draft->extents (:draft sub-draft) (:opts sub-draft)))))
[{:x ["w1" "w2"], :y [0.0 50.0]} {:x ["w1" "w2"], :y [0.0 105.0]}]

The extents of a group are pooled: numbers by the lowest low and the highest high, categories by listing every category of every cell. Each cell is then planned with the pooled extent in place of its own. The pooled extent is in the cell’s options in the plan:

(->> arranged-clinics
     pj/plan
     :sub-plots
     (mapv (fn [sub-plot] (:y-scale-domain (:opts sub-plot)))))
[[0.0 105.0] [0.0 105.0]]

Every cell pads that one extent the same way, so the panels end on one domain:

(->> arranged-clinics
     pj/plan
     :sub-plots
     (mapv (fn [sub-plot] (:y-domain (first (:panels (:plan sub-plot)))))))
[[0.0 110.25] [0.0 110.25]]

These details complete the picture:

  • Categories. Where the cells of a group are parts of one dataset, the pooled categories are listed in the order of that dataset’s rows, so the split has the axis of the same plot drawn without the split. Cells with data of their own are listed cell by cell.

  • Legends. A color legend and a shape legend follow the same rule: the categories of the legend are listed in the order of the rows of the dataset the panels are parts of. One function, pose/data-category-order, gives that order to the axis and to the legend. The palette, the order of a stack and the order of dodged marks follow the order of the legend.

  • A specified domain. A :domain that one cell specifies for the shared axis is the domain of every cell sharing that axis: every cell is planned as though it had specified that domain, so no cell pads the domain. On an axis of categories, the specified domain sets the order of the pooled categories. Cells that specify different domains for one shared axis report an error.

  • Text labels. A cell’s numeric domain is widened after planning so that its text marks are drawn in full, by an amount that depends on the cell’s own labels. Cells of a group that end on different domains are planned again with the widest domain as a floor, so that they agree.

  • Cost. A sharing cell’s stats run twice: once to measure it, and once to plan it with the pooled extent. A cell that shares with no other cell is not measured.

A facet in one plan follows the same steps inside pj/draft->plan: its panels are measured without padding, pooled, and each panel is then given the pooled extent and padded. The facet of the two clinics ends on the domain the arrangement ends on:

(->> faceted-clinics
     pj/plan
     :panels
     (mapv :y-domain))
[[0.0 110.25] [0.0 110.25]]

Poses rewritten before drafting

Some poses are rewritten into the cells they stand for before any of the above runs, so that one spelling cannot be drawn differently from another. pj/pose->draft does this in pose/expand-facet-nodes.

A facet over columns is kept on the pose as written, and expanded into a composite of one cell per column. A series faceted by the key column the series pivot adds asks for the same panels, so it is first rewritten into a facet over the columns of the series, and then expanded like any other, here on the weekly visits above:

(def series-by-key
  (-> weekly-visits
      (pj/lay-line :week [:adults :children])
      (pj/facet :series)))
series-by-key

The expanded pose is a composite. The column the layer drew along :x has moved to the root, and each cell names one of the series’ columns:

(-> series-by-key
    pose/expand-facet-nodes
    (dissoc :data)
    kind/pprint)
{:layers [{:layer-type :line, :mapping {}}],
 :mapping {:x :week},
 :layout {:direction :vertical},
 :poses
 [{:layout {:direction :horizontal},
   :poses
   [{:plotje/facet-cell true, :mapping {:y :adults}}
    {:plotje/facet-cell true, :mapping {:y :children}}]}]}

Each cell holds what the facet specified for it and nothing else. On the diagonal of a matrix, {:col {:x cols} :row {:y cols}}, a cell names one column on both axes, {:x :adults :y :adults}. A nil in a list of columns stays in the cell as a nil:

(->> (-> weekly-visits
         pj/pose
         (pj/facet {:col {:x [:adults nil]} :row {:y [:adults :children]}})
         pose/expand-facet-nodes)
     (tree-seq :poses :poses)
     (remove :poses)
     (mapv :mapping))
[{:y :adults, :x :adults}
 {:y :adults, :x nil}
 {:y :children, :x :adults}
 {:y :children, :x nil}]

The steps after this one read such a cell without a special case. pose/fit-layers keeps a layer in a cell where the layer names no column other than the cell’s and its layer type can draw from the number of distinct columns the cell names: one for {:x :adults :y :adults}, so a density fits and a scatter does not. Inference reads one column on both axes as one column and chooses a histogram, and the stat reads the column on :x and puts its count on :y. A bar, whose layer type can draw from one column or from two, counts the rows of each category of such a cell (resolve/infer-layer-type), and reports an error for a numerical column, as (pj/lay-bar data :adults) does. Written on one pose, (pj/lay-point data :adults :adults), a scatter draws the column against itself; in a cell of a facet it does not fit, and the cell is given a histogram.

A cell that no layer fits is left with no layer, and elaboration gives it the layer its columns choose. A layer that fits no cell is drawn in every cell, as a histogram written on a faceted scatter is. Where such a layer names a column on an axis on which every cell names another, and some cell would be left with no layer drawing that cell’s own columns, pose/fit-layers reports an error. On a two-by-two matrix, a scatter fits the two cells off the diagonal and a density fits the two cells on it:

(->> (-> (select-keys weekly-visits [:adults :children])
         pj/lay-point
         pj/lay-density
         (pj/facet {:col {:x [:adults :children]}
                    :row {:y [:adults :children]}}))
     pj/draft
     :sub-drafts
     (mapv (fn [sub-draft] (mapv :mark (:draft sub-draft)))))
[[:area] [:point] [:point] [:area]]

From here the pose is an ordinary composite: its cells are grouped, measured and planned as the two clinics above were. In the series faceted by its key, each cell draws a column of its own on :y, so by default the two cells share :x and not :y:

(->> series-by-key
     pj/draft
     :sub-drafts
     (mapv :share))
[{:x {:group 0}} {:x {:group 0}}]

Cells written by hand, each keeping the rows of one value of a column with :where, that together keep every value of the column are rewritten the other way, into one pose faceted by that column (pose/collapse-regular-split). A list that leaves a value out stays a composite. Here the three drive types of the mpg data plan as one faceted pose, and two of them as a composite:

(let [points (pj/lay-point (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) :displ :hwy)]
  (->> [[{:where {:drv "f"}} {:where {:drv "4"}} {:where {:drv "r"}}]
        [{:where {:drv "f"}} {:where {:drv "4"}}]]
       (mapv #(pj/composite-plan? (pj/plan (pj/arrange points %))))))
[false true]

Where a Mistake Is Reported

When a pose cannot be drawn, which step reports the error depends on what the error depends on. A call reports what its own arguments decide. pj/pose->draft reports what depends on which columns the data has, and on how the layers of a panel or the cells of a facet relate. pj/draft->plan reports what is known once a layer’s stat and mark meet the values of its columns – a bar given two categorical columns, a mark polar coordinates have no drawing for – and panels too small for the canvas. So pj/lay-point naming a column the data lacks returns a pose, and drafting that pose reports the column.

The table below builds a pose for each mistake and runs the steps in order. It shows the first step that reports an error, and the first sentence of the message:

(kind/table
 {:column-names ["Mistake" "Reported by" "First sentence of the message"]
  :row-vectors
  (for [[mistake build]
        [["A second column given to pj/lay-histogram"
          #(pj/lay-histogram weekly-visits :adults :children)]
         ["Pairs of columns given to pj/pose"
          #(pj/pose weekly-visits [[:week :adults] [:week :children]])]
         ["A key pj/facet's map does not accept"
          #(-> weekly-visits
               (pj/lay-point :week :adults)
               (pj/facet {:y [:adults :children] :z [:week]}))]
         ["A column the data lacks"
          #(pj/lay-point weekly-visits :week :teens)]
         ["A layer left without a column, on data of four columns"
          #(pj/lay-point (assoc weekly-visits :seniors [5 6 7 8]))]
         ["A category and a number on one axis"
          #(-> north
               (pj/lay-point :visits :week)
               (pj/lay-point :age :week))]
         ["A layer naming a column no cell of a facet over columns has"
          #(-> weekly-visits
               (pj/pose {:x :week})
               (pj/lay-point {:y :week})
               (pj/facet {:y [:adults :children]}))]
         ["A bar of two categorical columns"
          #(pj/lay-bar north :week :age)]
         ["A mark polar coordinates cannot draw"
          #(-> weekly-visits
               (pj/lay-line :week :adults)
               (pj/coord :polar))]
         ["Panels too small for the canvas"
          #(-> north
               (pj/lay-point :week :visits)
               (pj/facet :age)
               (pj/options {:width 60}))]]]
    (let [report (fn [step f]
                   (try (f)
                        nil
                        (catch Exception e
                          [mistake step (first (str/split (ex-message e) #"(?<=\.) "))])))
          pose (try (build) (catch Exception _ nil))]
      (or (report "the call" build)
          (report "pj/pose->draft" #(pj/pose->draft pose))
          (report "pj/draft->plan" #(pj/draft->plan (pj/pose->draft pose))))))})
Mistake Reported by First sentence of the message
A second column given to pj/lay-histogram the call pj/lay-histogram draws from one column, and was given :adults on :x and :children on :y.
Pairs of columns given to pj/pose the call pj/pose was given pairs of columns, [[:week :adults] [:week :children]].
A key pj/facet's map does not accept the call pj/facet was given {:y [:adults :children], :z [:week]}, and the map has unexpected key(s): [:z].
A column the data lacks pj/pose->draft Column :teens (from :y) not found in dataset.
A layer left without a column, on data of four columns pj/pose->draft pj/lay-point draws from two columns, one on :x and one on :y, and this layer has no column on :x or :y.
A category and a number on one axis pj/pose->draft The layers of this pose share one panel, and on :x they draw columns of different kinds: pj/lay-point draws :visits (numerical), pj/lay-point draws :age (categorical).
A layer naming a column no cell of a facet over columns has pj/pose->draft pj/lay-point names :week on :y, and no panel draws it: the panels draw :adults and :children on :y.
A bar of two categorical columns pj/draft->plan pj/lay-bar reads the length of a bar from a numerical column, but :week and :age are both categorical.
A mark polar coordinates cannot draw pj/draft->plan Mark :line is not supported with polar coordinates.
Panels too small for the canvas pj/draft->plan Each panel would be 11 wide, which is below the smallest panel size, 20.

The Plan Boundary

The plan is the first pipeline boundary: the boundary between description and rendering. The pose and draft stages assemble the description. The plan resolves it into computed geometry, domains, ticks, and legend – still as inspectable data, before any layout. The membrane and plot stages then produce the rendered output.

graph LR A["Pose + draft"] -->|plan| P["Plan"] P --> R["membrane + plot"] style A fill:#e8f5e9 style P fill:#fff3e0 style R fill:#e3f2fd

The plan is inspectable as data – Plan and PlanLayer records (which behave as maps), plain maps, numbers, strings, keywords, and dtype-next buffers for numeric arrays. It validates against a Malli schema.

This separation enables:

  • Inspecting the plan without rendering

  • Validating plot structure with Malli

  • Adding alternate backends that consume plans (SVG and raster are implemented today)

The Membrane Stage

The membrane is the second pipeline boundary: it separates data-space geometry from output-format bytes. The plan describes what to draw in data coordinates (e.g. a point at (3.4, 7.1) in the color for species setosa); the membrane describes the same content in drawing coordinates (e.g. a translation to (218, 134) carrying a colored shape). The plan is renderer-agnostic; the membrane is format-agnostic.

Clipping – keeping each panel’s marks within the panel – is an instance of this same translation. A panel’s domain, resolved at the plan stage, is a data-space fact: the range of values the panel shows. The membrane turns it into a drawing-space clip that hides any geometry reaching past that window, so a mark cannot paint outside its panel, or into a neighbor in a multi-panel layout. The Membranes chapter shows the mechanism; the Glossary has an entry for clip.

This boundary lets one membrane tree be rendered to many output formats. The pose, draft, plan, and membrane stages are reused unchanged across formats. A new format that consumes the membrane tree registers a defmethod on the render multimethod scicloj.plotje.impl.render/membrane->plot (the public pj/membrane->plot dispatches through it). A new format that goes from a plan directly to bytes (skipping membrane – e.g., a Plotly-spec target) registers a defmethod on scicloj.plotje.impl.render/plan->plot instead. The Extensibility chapter shows a worked backend registration.

The membrane stage of Plotje is built on Membrane – the library that defines the primitive types Plotje uses (Translate, WithColor, Path, Label, RoundedRectangle, …) and provides the rendering backends. Plotje constructs a membrane tree from a plan; Membrane renders it.

Backends Plotje wires into Membrane today:

  • SVG hiccup – the default. Renders in browsers, in notebooks via Kindly/Clay, and writes to .svg files.

  • Java2D / BufferedImage – raster output via Membrane’s Java2D backend. Used for .png files and any consumer that wants a Java image.

Membrane itself supports more rendering targets (terminal, native GUI, GL, …) than Plotje currently exposes. Wiring a new target into Plotje has not been done end-to-end yet – the defmethod registration is the extension point, but each backend has its own conventions for opts and interactivity that need to be worked out. As Membrane grows, Plotje can incorporate new targets without changing how plots are described.

Pipeline Summary

Stage Type Coordinates
Pose Plain map (leaf or composite) N/A (declarative)
Draft LeafDraft (:layers, :opts) or CompositeDraft (:sub-drafts, :chrome-spec, :layout, :width, :height) record N/A (declarative)
Plan Plan or CompositePlan record (with PlanLayer records and dtype buffers) Data space
Membrane Record tree (membrane.ui primitives in a vector) Drawing units
Plot Hiccup vector (:svg) or BufferedImage (:bufimg) Drawing units

Namespace Structure

graph TD API["api.clj"] --> POSE["impl/pose.clj"] API --> RES["impl/resolve.clj"] API --> PL["impl/plan.clj"] API --> COMP["impl/compositor.clj"] POSE --> RES COMP --> POSE COMP --> PL PL --> RES PL --> STAT["impl/stat.clj"] PL --> SCALE["impl/scale.clj"] PL --> DEFAULTS["impl/defaults.clj"] PL --> PS["impl/plan_schema.clj"] API --> RENDER["impl/render.clj"] RENDER --> SVG["render/svg.clj"] SVG --> MEMBRANE["render/membrane.clj"] MEMBRANE --> PANEL["render/panel.clj"] PANEL --> MARK["render/mark.clj"] PANEL --> SCALE PANEL --> COORD["impl/coord.clj"] API --> RC["render/composite.clj"] RC --> MEMBRANE style API fill:#c8e6c9 style COMP fill:#d1c4e9 style PL fill:#d1c4e9 style SVG fill:#f8bbd0 style MEMBRANE fill:#f8bbd0 style RC fill:#f8bbd0

impl/pose.clj holds the pose operations: resolve-tree (merges mappings, data and options from the root down to every leaf), elaborate (writes in what the draft chooses), expand-facet-nodes and fit-layers (a facet over columns as cells, and the layers each cell draws), shared-axis-groups (which cells share an axis), and leaf->draft (the leaf flattening that the public pj/pose->draft calls).

impl/compositor.clj handles composite framing layout, composite-pose->draft, and composite-draft->plan – pure data-side, no membrane dependency.

impl/plan.clj holds the leaf-plan computation (domains, ticks, legends, layout) that the public pj/draft->plan calls.

impl/resolve.clj defines the Plan, CompositePlan, LeafDraft, CompositeDraft, PlanLayer, and LayerType records, and holds resolve-draft-layer (single draft layer resolution, column type inference, grouping).

The impl/ directory is pure data with no membrane dependency. The render/ directory uses membrane for layout and SVG/raster conversion. render/composite.clj carries the composite plan->membrane defmethod and the membrane drawables for composite framing (title, strip labels, shared legend).

Dependencies

Plotje builds on several Clojure libraries:

  • Tablecloth & dtype-next – dataset manipulation and high-performance numeric arrays

  • Membrane – rendering and layout

  • Wadogo – scales

  • Clojure2d – color palettes and gradients

  • Fastmath – statistics

  • Malli – schema validation

  • Kindly & Clay – notebook rendering
